title: Software development
description: Ten real engineering problems, two per lane: design, code, test, review and fix. Judge-scored 0-100.

values.label: Design
values.description: Given a problem and the code as it stood, write a design doc.

values.label: Code
values.description: Given an approved design, implement it with tests.

values.label: Test
values.description: Given a working implementation, write the test suite.

values.label: Review
values.description: Given a change later found to be faulty, review it.

values.label: Fix
values.description: Given a symptom, find the root cause and fix it with a regression test.

metrics.label: Judge score
metrics.description: Mean of six blind judges, 0-100 (may include up to +10 novelty bonus).

metrics.label: Rubric
metrics.description: Structured rubric score from the two scorers.

metrics.label: Claude judges
metrics.description: Mean of the three Claude Opus 5.5 judges.

metrics.label: GPT judges
metrics.description: Mean of the three GPT-6 Astra judges.

metrics.label: Judge spread
metrics.description: Standard deviation of the six judges' scores.

metrics.label: Mean rank
metrics.description: Mean within-exercise rank given by the judges (1 = best).

metrics.label: Cost
metrics.description: List-price cost of the run (reported or estimated; see seat).

metrics.label: All gates
metrics.description: Every mechanical gate passed (build, lints, hidden tests, parity, speed...).

metrics.label: Hidden tests
metrics.description: Share of hidden tests passed (code exercises).

metrics.label: Parity
metrics.description: Differential parity against the interpreter held (recompiler exercises).

metrics.label: Speed gate
metrics.description: The timed benchmark showed a gain separated from noise (performance exercises).

metrics.label: Speed vs reference
metrics.description: Speed gain as a share of the historical reference fix's gain (performance exercises).

scoring: Each exercise is a real problem from the history of two private projects (a PC emulator and a hobby OS kernel), rewound to the commit before it was solved, with anything that would give the answer away removed.

Three layers of scoring. Gates are scripts: it builds, lints are clean, hidden tests pass, planted bugs are caught, and for performance exercises a timed benchmark plus a parity check. A rubric is then filled in by two scorers, one Claude and one GPT, who must cite evidence. Finally a blind panel of six judges sees every seat's output under shuffled labels, with the rubric sheets, and gives each a 0-100 score; a judge may depart from the rubric with a reason and may add up to +10 for something good the rubric missed.
The score here is the mean of the six judges. Spread is the standard deviation across judges; the Claude-judge and GPT-judge means are shown separately.
The headline is a seat-by-lane table, not one overall winner: two exercises per lane is too few to call a lane, let alone a model.
caveats: Seat = model + effort + harness. Claude seats run in Claude Code, GPT seats in the Codex CLI, so model and harness are confounded.
Seats run with the fleet's own agent configuration (instructions, skills and hooks), not a vanilla install of Claude Code or the Codex CLI.
All runs used the fleet's subscription logins except the older API baselines (GPT-4o, o3, GPT-5), which ran pay-per-token on the OpenAI API with a per-run cost cap.

Cost is a list-price figure, not what was paid. Claude Code reports its own list-price cost; the Codex CLI reports only tokens, so GPT costs are estimates from token counts at published list prices (standard tier; one price was taken from third-party trackers).
One capped Opus 4.5 run (FIX-01) reported no cost; its figure is estimated from transcript tokens at list price.

Judging is not fully independent of the seats: the panel is three Claude Opus 5.5 and three GPT-6 Astra judges, so Opus and Astra outputs were judged in part by their own model (blind, but not by another family only).
Performance exercises were timed as 5 base/seat pairs on a machine that was also doing other work; the gate checks the gain is separated from noise, but absolute times are not lab-grade.
Some Claude runs hit a usage limit and were resumed in the same session (flagged resumed); their cost is the session's total, including the context re-read on resume.
A run that stopped early (no tool calls, or under two minutes) without hitting a cap was told to continue, up to three times (flagged nudged); its time and cost include every part.
FIX-01: most seats fail the hidden display-register test (all six phase-1 seats did), so All gates shows fail for them; the judge score reflects how much of the fix each seat got right.

COD-01: the seats were timed in five groups (six, six, the two Sol medium/max seats, the four seats added on 18 Nov, on a near-idle box, then three of the four seats added on 19 Nov; GPT-5 high was not timed because it fails parity, so its speed scores 0 by rule) on different days on a shared machine; the speed gate holds for each, but speed-of-reference fractions across groups are not strictly comparable. Sol max was re-timed once because its first timing ran under about three times the load the others had; the first attempt is kept in its record.
FIX-02: Haiku's speed gain (1.15 of the reference) was timed under heavy machine load; every timing pair was faster, so its speed gate pass stands, but the size of the gain is uncertain.

COD-02: one helper in the hidden tests failed to compile for seats that gave the volume type a cleanup (Drop) step, scoring them 0 for the test file rather than their code; the helper was fixed and all 14 seats were re-graded on the revised file.
One run per seat per exercise so far; the design calls for three runs on design exercises, which will show as spread when they land.
